name: Low-orbit satellite broadband
title: Why Teledesic failed, and when satellite broadband became viable
question: Why did Teledesic fail, and when did low-orbit satellite internet become viable?
answer: Teledesic (1990), backed by Craig McCaw and Bill Gates, planned hundreds of low-orbit satellites for global internet and suspended work in 2002. At Space Shuttle-era launch prices, about $54,500 per kilogram by NASA's estimate, a constellation could not pay back. Falcon 9 advertised about $2,720/kg; SpaceX started Starlink in 2015.
verdict_reason: Reusable-era launch prices fell about 20x; Starlink followed.

constraint.name: Launch cost per kilogram
constraint.detail: A broadband constellation needs thousands of satellites replaced every few years; launch cost decides whether it pays.

crossing.text: Falcon 9 first flight; advertised price about $2,720/kg to LEO.

metric.label: Cost to launch one kilogram to low Earth orbit (NASA estimate, 2018)
metric.note: Two points from one NASA paper: Space Shuttle (first flight 1981) at about $54,500/kg and Falcon 9 (first flight 2010) at its advertised $2,720/kg. Advertised prices are list prices, not audited costs.

evidence.text: NASA: the Space Shuttle cost about $54,500/kg to LEO; Falcon 9 advertises $2,720/kg, a factor of 20.
